channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: India's finance minister said the IMF expects the economy to pass USD 5 trillion by FY29 and consumption to reach USD 1.9 trillion by 2030, yet the manufacturing PMI slowed to a near five-year low and pharma cut its 2030 export target.
item.description:
India's data cut both ways. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the IMF projects India crossing the USD 5-trillion mark in fiscal 2029 on a broad-based growth strategy, and a FICCI–Deloitte study forecast private consumption reaching nearly USD 1.9 trillion by 2030 on rising incomes and digital adoption. But the near-term momentum cooled: India's manufacturing PMI slowed to its weakest in almost five years, though it stayed in expansion. The pharmaceutical industry trimmed its 2030 sales expectation to USD 80–90 billion, well below the USD 130 billion target set in 2025, blaming tariff and shipping headwinds. Housing was a bright spot, with capital values and rental yields rising in tandem across the top 11 markets since 2019, even as affordable housing remained a gap. The overall read is a large, fast-growing economy whose long-run trajectory is intact but whose short-run industrial pulse has softened.

Industry Impact

India is one of the most important structural growth markets for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants, driven by construction, autos, packaging and manufacturing, so the long-run consumption and GDP trajectory is strongly positive for ACS demand. The near-term factory slowdown and the pharma sector's tariff-and-shipping-driven downgrade are cautionary — a reminder that global trade disruption (a running theme in this alert) is reaching even resilient India. Rising housing values support construction-chemicals demand. For ACS planners the balance favours continued investment in Indian capacity for the medium term while watching the manufacturing PMI and trade frictions for shorter-term volume signals.

New Indian Express | Business Standard | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | Business Recorder | South China Morning Post

item.title: US construction spending fell 3.2% year-on-year in June, with commercial building down sharply and factory orders slipping, yet manufacturing expanded for a seventh straight month and analysts still expect a Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end.
item.description:
The US picture was mixed but tilting cautious. Construction spending fell 3.2% year-on-year and 0.1% month-on-month to an annualised USD 2.17 trillion in June, dragged down by commercial building (down 5.3%), even though nonresidential spending edged up 0.1% on data-centre strength. Factory new orders slipped 0.3% in June after a 1.1% May fall. The labour-force participation rate dropped to 61.6%, partly a statistical population revision but also a genuine softening. Set against that, the Institute for Supply Management's factory index hit 55.6 in July — the strongest since 2022 and a seventh consecutive month of expansion, with manufacturing payrolls stabilising after heavy earlier losses. Because that manufacturing strength coincides with war-driven energy inflation, analysts increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to nudge interest rates up by about a quarter point by the end of 2026 rather than cut — an unusual stance late in a cycle.

Industry Impact

Construction is a core ACS end-market, so a 3.2% annual drop in US building spending — concentrated in commercial — is a demand warning for adhesives, sealants and coatings tied to that segment, only partly offset by data-centre-driven strength. The divergence between soft construction and firm manufacturing means ACS suppliers weighted toward industrial and electronics applications may fare better than those exposed to commercial construction. A Fed leaning toward a hike rather than a cut keeps financing costs elevated for building and capital projects, reinforcing the case for a cautious near-term demand outlook in US construction-linked ACS lines.

Associated General Contractors | Dünya | Associated Builders and Contractors | Dünya | Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis | Axios | Commercial Times

item.title: Brazil rejected Washington's decision to revoke its US ambassador's visa, calling it clear election interference, as 80-year-old President Lula launched his fourth-term campaign and a poll put him in a technical dead heat with Flavio Bolsonaro.
item.description:
The US–Brazil relationship frayed further. Brazil's government formally rejected the US decision to revoke the visa of its ambassador in Washington, Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti, calling it a clear attempt to interfere in Brazil's internal affairs — a fresh diplomatic rupture between the Trump administration and Lula's government. It comes as the domestic race tightens: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, said he was "in great shape" as he launched his bid for a fourth and final term, and was formally nominated by his Workers' Party. A Nexus/BTG Pactual poll, however, showed a statistical tie for a likely runoff — Lula on 46% against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on 45% — with Bolsonaro closing the gap. The combination of an external clash with Washington and a knife-edge domestic contest raises the political temperature in Latin America's largest economy heading into the autumn.

Industry Impact

Brazil is a significant Latin American market for construction chemicals, coatings and adhesives, and political and diplomatic uncertainty tends to weigh on the currency and on investment decisions. A US–Brazil trade or diplomatic escalation could disrupt bilateral flows and add currency volatility that complicates pricing and sourcing for ACS operations in the region. A tight, polarised election also clouds the 2027 policy outlook — from industrial and trade policy to environmental rules affecting bio-based feedstocks. For now the practical implication is heightened country risk to factor into Latin American planning rather than an immediate operational hit.

Lianhe Zaobao | La Nacion | MarketScreener | South China Morning Post | China Daily

item.title: Chinese car brands lifted their share of new-car sales in 18 West-European countries to a record 10.7% in the second quarter, nearly double a year earlier, while German premium makers battled a profit squeeze and Tesla's China-built sales jumped 38%.
item.description:
The balance of Europe's car market kept tilting east. Chinese brands such as BYD and Xpeng raised their combined share of new-car sales across 18 West-European markets to a record 10.7% in April–June, up from 5.7% a year earlier, per Schmidt Automotive Research; Tesla's regional share also rose. In their home market the Chinese majors kept scaling — Leapmotor delivered over 101,000 vehicles in July (up 102% year-on-year), BYD sold 411,000, and Chery said it had passed 20 million cumulative global sales and now exports more than 200,000 vehicles a month. Tesla's China-made EV sales rose 37.8% to 93,579 units in July, including exports. German incumbents, by contrast, are under strain: a Handelsblatt analysis found the core passenger-car margins of BMW and Mercedes have in part fallen below those of mass-market makers, and commentators warned the German industry is "losing its rhythm" by defending the combustion engine while China sets the pace on batteries and software. French suppliers Forvia, Valeo and OPmobility were a relative bright spot, posting resilient first-half results; Volvo's sales fell 4%.

Industry Impact

The automotive shift reshapes where ACS demand sits. As Chinese EV makers take European share and dominate at home, the adhesives, battery-pack bonding, thermal-interface materials and coatings that go into cars increasingly get specified by Chinese OEMs and their supply chains — a challenge for ACS firms whose relationships are with struggling European incumbents. The resilience of French Tier-1 suppliers shows where value is still being captured in Europe. ACS producers should deepen qualification with the ascendant EV platforms (Chinese and Tesla-China) while managing exposure to shrinking German premium volumes.

South China Morning Post | The Economic Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | Business Recorder | Handelsblatt | Les Echos | MarketScreener

item.title: New-home prices across 100 Chinese cities rose about 2% year-on-year in July, an unusual off-season gain, and economists see room for further rate and reserve-ratio cuts, though a German business lobby saw no real demand rebound yet.
item.description:
China's most troubled sector flickered to life. Average new-home prices in 100 cities rose 2.09% year-on-year and 0.26% month-on-month in July, an atypical increase for a quiet season, according to the China Index Academy; existing-home transactions in 20 key cities were up 9.3% on the year, even if down month-on-month — tentative evidence that Beijing's support measures are steadying the market. Policy support looks set to continue: UBS's chief China economist said the central bank still has room to cut interest rates and the reserve requirement ratio (the share of deposits banks must hold back) to lower financing costs, and the National Development and Reform Commission said it is urgently drafting a 2026–30 plan to expand domestic demand. Xi Jinping made a symbolic visit to Shanghai to address housing concerns. But the caveats were loud: the German Chamber of Commerce in North China said there is no sign of a significant near-term pickup in Chinese demand, noting the new five-year plan still tilts toward the supply side. Chinese outbound direct investment, meanwhile, grew 7.1% in 2025 to USD 174 billion.

Industry Impact

Chinese construction and property are major end-markets for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants — tile adhesives, sealants, waterproofing and architectural coatings — so even a tentative price stabilisation matters for demand sentiment. But the split signals argue for caution: prices firming while a business lobby sees no demand rebound suggests any recovery is policy-propped and uneven. Continued rate and reserve cuts would ease conditions for construction activity. For ACS suppliers the practical read is to watch volume (transactions and starts) rather than headline prices, and to note that a supply-side-tilted five-year plan may favour industrial over consumer-facing construction demand.

China Economic Net | Caijing | China Daily | China Economic Net | Chinatimes | China Daily | The Diplomat

item.title: France faces up to EUR 15 billion in wildfire losses after evacuating 220,000 people, the Danube fell low enough to expose WWII wrecks, Italy raised its Po Valley drought emergency to "high", and Hungary's only nuclear plant faced cooling-water strain.
item.description:
The European summer hardened into a broad economic shock. A ratings agency estimated France's total wildfire losses at EUR 10–15 billion after unprecedented fires forced around 220,000 evacuations, exposing a wide gap between total and insured losses. Drought gripped the continent: the Danube on the Serbia–Romania border dropped so low that sunken World War II warships re-emerged near a Serbian port; Italy's Po River Basin Authority raised its drought emergency to "high", with more than 100 northern municipalities facing drinking-water problems and agriculture "on its knees"; Austria reported crop failures and emergency livestock slaughter; and in Hungary, extreme heat cut Danube levels enough to threaten cooling water at the Paks nuclear plant, a pillar of the grid. Spain, meanwhile, is on course to waste a record amount of renewable power as solar and wind output outruns demand and grid capacity. Overarching it all, a strengthening "Super El Niño" weather pattern pushed a key agricultural-commodity index to a three-year high, and the British Retail Consortium and farmers' groups warned of higher food prices ahead.

Industry Impact

The immediate ACS-relevant channel is logistics and energy. Low Rhine and Danube levels raise barge freight costs and can throttle chemical shipments in and out of Europe's industrial core (a risk quantified in insight 3). Power-supply stress — plants curtailed by cooling-water shortages even as Spain dumps surplus renewables — points to continued volatile European energy costs. Drought-hit agriculture also lifts prices for bio-based feedstocks and packaging demand patterns. For ACS producers the message is that climate disruption is now a recurring operational-cost factor in Europe, not a one-off, arguing for resilient logistics routing and energy hedging through the summer.

MarketScreener | AP | Il Sole 24 Ore | China Economic Net | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | ABC | Handelsblatt

item.title: Japan will impose provisional anti-dumping duties of up to 55.3% on hot-dip galvanised steel from China and South Korea from 8 August, while India extended anti-dumping duties on four chemical and metal products and added a new one.
item.description:
Trade-defence walls kept rising in Asia. Japan's finance and industry ministries announced provisional anti-dumping duties — extra import taxes meant to offset goods sold abroad below fair value — of between 29.2% and 55.3% on hot-dip galvanised steel sheet (zinc-coated steel used in cars, appliances and construction) from China and South Korea, running from 8 August to 7 December while a final decision is prepared, to shield Japanese mills from low-priced imports. India moved on a parallel track, extending existing anti-dumping duties on four products — untreated fumed silica, arylides (a pigment class), certain seamless steel tubes and normal butanol (a solvent) — and imposing a new duty on another, on the recommendation of its trade-remedies authority. India's government also acknowledged nine trade disputes pending against it at the World Trade Organization and heard industry complaints that slow anti-dumping enforcement is hurting local producers. Together the moves show governments increasingly reaching for targeted import taxes to defend domestic industry.

Industry Impact

Several of these measures touch ACS inputs directly: fumed silica is a common rheology-control additive in adhesives, sealants and coatings; arylides are colourants; and butanol is a widely used solvent and coating intermediate. Anti-dumping duties on such inputs raise costs or force requalification of suppliers for formulators sourcing from the affected exporters. More broadly, galvanised-steel duties reshape the metals that coatings and construction chemicals are applied to. The pattern reinforces this alert's central theme — a fragmenting trade system where ACS producers must map exposure input by input and keep alternative, duty-free sources qualified.

Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | MarketScreener | The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times

item.title: A new World Bank report said AI could let developing countries gain a century's worth of development in a decade if they close power, connectivity and skills gaps, finding just 4.5% of their jobs exposed to automation, far below richer economies.
item.description:
The World Bank struck an unusually optimistic note for emerging markets. Its World Development Report 2026, "Decoding AI for Development", argues that artificial intelligence offers developing countries a historic chance to accelerate growth — potentially "a century's worth of development in a decade" — if they move fast to fix power supply, connectivity and skills. Crucially, it finds the feared wave of job losses is smaller in poorer economies: only about 4.5% of jobs in low- and middle-income countries are exposed to automation by generative AI, versus 14.2% in high-income ones, because their job mix is less office-based. India is highlighted as a leading adopter, with examples such as AI tools saving small farmers money. The Bank does warn of downside where youth unemployment is high, singling out Pakistan and the wider Middle East–North Africa region as more vulnerable. The report lands amid a burst of Chinese AI supply: five major new models arrived in eight weeks — Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max, Moonshot's Kimi K3, ByteDance's Seedance, DeepSeek's V4 Flash and Zhipu's GLM-5.2 — while China's intelligent-computing capacity jumped 177% year-on-year.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers the signal is about where demand and productivity growth will come from. Faster AI-driven development in India, Southeast Asia and other emerging markets supports construction, manufacturing and consumer demand — the end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants — and points to where capacity and commercial focus may shift over the decade. Internally, cheap and rapidly improving AI (including low-cost open models from China) is a practical tool for formulation research, quality control and supply-chain optimisation. The competitive question is whether Western firms adopt these tools as quickly as the emerging-market customers the World Bank expects to leap ahead.

MarketScreener | Anadolu Agency | China Daily | The Economic Times | Business Recorder | Commercial Times

item.title: China issued its first mandatory national safety standards for advanced self-driving cars, covering the whole design-to-operation lifecycle and requiring a manual override from July 2027, as it also tightened chip-design protection.
item.description:
Beijing moved to regulate an industry it is racing to lead. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology unveiled the country's first mandatory national safety standards for vehicles with conditional or high automation — so-called Level 3 and Level 4 systems, where the car drives itself under set conditions but may still need a human backup. The rules impose full-lifecycle safety management across design, development, manufacturing and operation, and require a mandatory deactivation override; they take effect on 1 July 2027. In a related tightening of its tech rulebook, Premier Li Qiang signed revised regulations protecting integrated-circuit (chip) layout designs, raising registration standards and allowing punitive damages for infringement. Chinese players are pushing outward at the same time: Pony.ai's chief laid out a roadmap to launch autonomous-taxi pilots in France and Europe within a year or two, and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang open-sourced a new self-driving model, Alpamayo 2, aimed at trucks, robotaxis and buses — signs that both regulation and competition in autonomous mobility are accelerating.

Industry Impact

Clear safety rules tend to unlock scale, and mass deployment of autonomous and electric vehicles is a direct opportunity for ACS suppliers: sensor bonding, battery-pack adhesives and thermal management, structural bonding for lightweight bodies, and protective coatings for electronics all rise with automation content per vehicle. China setting the first binding standard positions its supply chain to shape global norms, which matters for Western ACS makers deciding whether to design to Chinese specifications. The parallel chip-design and export moves are a reminder that the automotive-electronics value chain is becoming another arena of technological competition.

Anadolu Agency | The Straits Times | The Standard | Channel News Asia | Le Parisien | Cnyes

item.title: Japan's Cabinet adopted its 2026 defence white paper, naming China its biggest strategic challenge and setting a harder agenda of combat drones, AI-enabled warfare and expanded arms exports, as Germany reaffirmed its own push to become "war-ready".
item.description:
Japan formalised a tougher posture. On 4 August the Cabinet approved a 598-page defence white paper that again names China as Japan's greatest strategic challenge, citing the growing frequency of Chinese warships in the Pacific. The document is notably harder than past editions: it calls for longer-range missiles and counterstrike capability, urges rapid adoption of drones and artificial intelligence as central to "new ways of warfare" — drawing lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East — and says Japan must expand arms exports, strengthen its defence-industrial base and deepen ties with security partners to reinforce deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. It explicitly flags building combat drones. The move dovetails with a broader Western rearmament theme: in Germany, Chancellor Merz and Defence Minister Pistorius restated their goal of making the country "war-ready" within a few years, though the Bundeswehr remains far from its target of 260,000 active soldiers.

Industry Impact

Sustained, structural rises in defence spending across Japan and Europe pull through to materials demand. Drones, missiles, counterstrike systems and a rebuilt defence-industrial base all consume high-performance adhesives, sealants, structural bonding and protective and electronics coatings — a durable growth vector for ACS suppliers with aerospace and defence qualifications. Japan's explicit call to expand arms exports could also open new customer markets. The flip side is tighter scrutiny and possible export controls on dual-use chemicals and advanced materials, so ACS players serving defence should expect both rising demand and heavier compliance requirements.

The Mainichi | Japan Today | The Nation | The Mainichi | The Independent | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The head of safety-equipment maker Drägerwerk warned that Germany's chemical industry is in a quiet decline under high energy costs and weak demand, as a separate institute cautioned that low river levels alone could shave 0.4 points off German output.
item.description:
A pointed warning came from close to the shop floor. Stefan Dräger, who runs Lübeck-based Drägerwerk — a supplier of measuring devices, gas-warning systems and respiratory protection to chemical plants — said Germany's chemical industry is "dying quietly", squeezed between high energy prices and soft demand, with too little public attention on the erosion. Because Dräger sells into the sector, its own order book is an early indicator of how chemical customers are investing, giving the warning added weight. The message compounds a run of bad news for the German industrial base: the German Economic Institute (IW) warned that persistently low water levels on the Rhine and other rivers could cut national economic output by 0.4 percentage points, enough to erase this year's growth, because barges cannot move normal cargo volumes. Not every signal was negative — French floral-packaging maker Clayrton's is investing over EUR 7 million in a new logistics site — but the dominant tone from Germany was of a core industry slipping.

Industry Impact

This is the ACS heartland. Germany is the centre of Europe's Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants supply base, and a "quiet death" narrative — high power costs, weak demand, deferred investment — describes exactly the pressure on the resins, solvents and specialty-chemical suppliers that ACS producers depend on. Combined with the river-transport warning, which raises inbound and outbound logistics costs across the Rhine corridor, the risk is a slow loss of European upstream capacity that leaves ACS makers more dependent on imports and more exposed to the very trade barriers going up elsewhere in this alert. Watching supplier capital-spending signals like Dräger's is a useful early-warning gauge.

Handelsblatt | WirtschaftsWoche | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Tagesschau | Les Echos

item.title: Trump opened new trade-war fronts — invoking a rare 1930s tariff law against Canada, preparing tariffs on Chinese polysilicon and drafting a ban on Chinese data-centre parts — even as 25 states sue to overturn his main tariffs on 60 economies.
item.description:
Rather than one tariff wall, several are now going up at once. Washington invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act — a long-dormant clause that lets the president penalise countries deemed to discriminate against US commerce — to place new duties on a range of Canadian exports, and Trump separately threatened fresh tariffs on Canadian alcohol from 19 August. The administration is also preparing tariffs plus a minimum "price floor" on polysilicon, the refined silicon used in solar panels and semiconductors, to shield US producers Wacker Chemie and Hemlock Semiconductor from Chinese rivals; and it is drafting a ban on imports of Chinese-made optical transceivers, the components that shuttle data inside data centres, at the urging of the Federal Communications Commission. On top of that, Pakistan was hit with an extra 10% duty over its existing 29% rate. All of this lands while 25 Democratic-led states press a lawsuit in the US trade court to strike down the flagship 10–12.5% "forced-labour" tariffs on about 60 economies, arguing the White House overreached after the Supreme Court voided its earlier tariffs — leaving the whole regime under legal doubt even as it expands. One firm, Global Industrial, reported USD 21 million in refunds of earlier emergency-power (IEEPA) tariffs.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS supply chains this is a widening, not a narrowing, of trade risk. The polysilicon move directly touches a chemical value chain and signals Washington's willingness to use raw-material tariffs plus price floors as strategic tools — a template that could reach other feedstocks. The Section 338 action against Canada threatens cross-border inputs (paper, packaging, solvents) in tightly integrated North American chains. And because the courts may yet strike the main tariffs down, firms face the hardest planning problem of all: duties that are simultaneously expanding and legally reversible, arguing for flexible sourcing and contractual tariff-pass-through clauses.

Printing United Alliance | The Economic Times | The Daily Mail | The Globe and Mail | Dawn | Politico | MarketScreener

item.title: Oil turned higher as US–Iran peace talks produced no concrete result and a cargo ship was struck near the Strait of Hormuz, reversing the prior day's dip, while the eight biggest listed oil producers booked almost USD 93 billion in quarterly profit.
item.description:
The brief relief rally faded. Brent crude climbed back above USD 84 a barrel as traders concluded that the much-touted US–Iran talks were yielding nothing firm and that the war could re-escalate; global equity markets turned mixed on the same worry. Overnight, a cargo ship was hit by an unknown projectile near Al Khasab, at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz — the sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil — keeping the chokepoint tense. Saudi Aramco's chief executive said the war has cost the market more than 2.6 billion barrels of lost supply since February, nearly a month of normal global output, and the company is now weighing options to expand export capacity to work around the disruption. The Hong Kong Shipowners' Association estimates 70 to 80 of its members' vessels, with up to 1,600 crew, remain trapped in or near the conflict zone. Against that backdrop the "Big Oil" majors — Aramco, BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, Chevron, Exxon and others — reported almost USD 93 billion in second-quarter profit, up from about USD 50 billion a year earlier; BP alone more than doubled its profit to USD 5.7 billion.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, the takeaway is that yesterday's hope of cost relief has not arrived: crude is back up, Hormuz is still contested and tanker risk remains extreme, so naphtha, solvent, resin and freight costs stay elevated and volatile. The record oil-major margins confirm the pain is still concentrated upstream and has not eased for downstream chemical buyers. Procurement should keep hedges and buffer stocks in place and treat any single-day oil drop as noise until a Hormuz reopening is actually confirmed.

Anadolu Agency | AP | The Guardian | BBC News | BNN Bloomberg | Hong Kong Commercial Daily | Financial Post
